I'm running into a peer dependency resolution bug in pnpm.

*   The resolvePeers function must handle the 'peer diamond' scenario: when a package peer-depends on both package A and package B, and package A also peer-depends on package B, the resolver must ensure A and B resolve to a mutually consistent version of their shared peer.

*   When a nested plugin peer-depends on both a parser and a shared runtime, and the parser also peer-depends on that runtime, the resulting dependenciesGraph must contain the dep path where both the plugin and its parser resolve to the same runtime version (e.g., 'plugin/1.0.0(parser/1.0.0(typescript/1.0.0))(typescript/1.0.0)').

*   The dependenciesGraph must NOT contain a dep path where the plugin's parser resolves to a different runtime version than the plugin itself (e.g., the path 'plugin/1.0.0(parser/1.0.0(typescript/2.0.0))(typescript/1.0.0)' must be absent).

*   When a top-level instance of a package (e.g., parser resolved against runtime@2.0.0) conflicts with a nested instance of the same package (e.g., parser resolved against runtime@1.0.0 within an app subtree), the nested sibling package that peer-depends on both must use the locally consistent instance, not the top-level hoisted instance.

*   An end-to-end install of packages forming the peer diamond pattern must produce a lockfile containing exactly one snapshot for the plugin package: the snapshot where all shared peers are consistent with the plugin's own peer resolutions.


*   Interface details: Type: Function
Name: resolvePeers
Location: installing/deps-resolver/src/resolvePeers.ts
Signature: resolvePeers(opts: ResolvePeersOptions) -> Promise<{ dependenciesGraph: DependenciesGraph, ... }>
Description: Resolves peer dependencies across the entire dependency tree. Given a dependency tree map and project roots, computes the deduplicated dependency graph with peer-resolved suffixes as keys. Must be fixed so that when a package peer-depends on two packages A and B, and A also peer-depends on B, the resolved dep path for that package always shows A and B agreeing on the same version of their shared peer B — not an inherited instance of A that resolved B at a different version.

Parameters accepted in the options object:
- allPeerDepNames: Set<string> — names of all peer dependencies in the graph
- projects: Array of project descriptors, each with directNodeIdsByAlias (Map<string, NodeId>), topParents (array), rootDir (ProjectRootDir), and id (string)
- resolvedImporters: object
- dependenciesTree: Map<NodeId, DependenciesTreeNode<PartialResolvedPackage>> — the full dependency tree; each node has children (Record<string, NodeId>), installable (boolean), resolvedPackage (PartialResolvedPackage with name, pkgIdWithPatchHash, version, peerDependencies, id fields), and depth (number)
- virtualStoreDir: string
- virtualStoreDirMaxLength: number
- lockfileDir: string
- peersSuffixMaxLength: number
- workspaceProjectIds: Set<string>

Return value: Promise resolving to an object containing dependenciesGraph, whose keys are peer-resolved dep path strings of the form 'pkg/version(peer1/version(peer2/version))(peer3/version)'.

The verification system will apply test patches automatically.
Your task is to implement the feature in source files only.

Here's what I found on how pnpm resolves peer dependencies and the "diamond" scenario where a shared peer dependency can be linked to the wrong version.

## How peer resolution works in pnpm

pnpm treats peer dependencies differently from regular dependencies. Peer dependencies are resolved from dependencies installed higher in the dependency graph, since they share the same version as their parent. This is the "propagate parent packages down the chain" behavior you're referencing.

Because of this, a package with peers can end up with **multiple distinct dependency sets**. If foo@1.0.0 has two peers (bar@^1 and baz@^1) then it might have multiple different sets of dependencies in the same project. foo@1.0.0 is installed for foo-parent-1 and foo-parent-2. Both packages have bar and baz as well, but they depend on different versions of baz. As a result, foo@1.0.0 has two different sets of dependencies: one with baz@1.0.0 and the other one with baz@1.1.0.

## The `parentPkgsMatch` / diamond scenario

The internal resolution walk you mentioned is described in pnpm's resolver. The resolve_peers function (port of pnpm's resolvePeers) performs a depth-first walk of the dependencies tree, propagating available parent packages down the chain to match against peerDependencies.

The mechanism that decides which parent version gets used is the parent-refs map. The ParentRefs map tracks available peer dependency candidates as the tree is traversed. It maps a package name to a list of available versions (to handle multiple occurrences of the same package name at different depths). When there are multiple versions of the same peer package present (a diamond), the walker's matching logic (`parentPkgsMatch`) determines whether variants can share a resolution — and when the walker descends into children, it adds the current package to the ParentRefs map, ensuring that siblings can resolve peers from each other if they are hoisted, or from their common ancestors.

## Known bugs where the wrong version is linked

This exact class of problem — a shared peer being linked to the wrong version — has been reported multiple times:

- **Monorepo, multiple versions present (#7976):** Even though in package-b, rollup-plugin-visualizer has a peerDep on rollup v2 or v3, pnpm links it with rollup v4 which is installed by package-a in the repo. pnpm v9 doesn't seem to respect the peer dependency version as made explicit by some package if there are multiple versions of that peer dependency already in the monorepo.

- **Exact-version peer picked wrong (#8799):** In this case vitest declares an exact peer of `@vitest/browser: "2.1.5"`, yet it shows @vitest/browser 2.1.4 as peer of vitest 2.1.5, which is wrong. The package.json in vitest is using exact version 2.1.5. Notably, deleting node_modules doesn't work either — you have to delete the lock file to get it to install 2.1.5. This points to stale lockfile resolution as a contributing factor.

- **auto-install-peers picking wrong version (#5373):** With `auto-install-peers=true` and an exact peer of `rxjs: "6.6.7"`, the user gets rxjs version 7.5.6 and does not get any warning that the installed dependency does not match the version specified.

## Relevant dedupe behavior

The "diamond collapse" behavior is also affected by deduplication. When dedupe_peer_dependents is enabled (default true), pnpm optimizes the graph by merging peer-suffixed variants. Specifically, if one variant of a package satisfies a superset of the peer requirements of another compatible variant, the smaller one is collapsed into the larger one. If the "superset" match is computed too loosely, this dedupe step can be a place where a variant ends up pointing at a peer version that doesn't strictly match its declared range.

## Practical workarounds

If you're hitting the wrong-version-linked problem:

1. **Delete the lockfile and reinstall**, since stale lockfile entries were the trigger in issue #8799.
2. **Use `overrides`** to force a single version — this field allows you to instruct pnpm to override any dependency in the dependency graph, including peer dependencies, useful for enforcing all your packages to use a single version of a dependency. Note that the overrides field can only be set at the root of the project.
3. Be aware that when requirements genuinely conflict, pnpm will not install any version of the conflicting peer dependency automatically; instead, a warning is printed.

The fix is complete. Here's a summary of what I did.

## The bug

In `resolvePeers.ts`, when descending into a node's children, the resolver merges the child's peer-dependency packages into the inherited (ancestor) scope. The merge used `parentPkgsMatch`, which treats two instances of a package as interchangeable whenever they share the same **name and version** — ignoring how each resolves *its own* peer dependencies.

That breaks the peer-diamond case (`plugin → parser`, `plugin → typescript`, `parser → typescript`): a top-level `parser` that resolved `typescript@2.0.0` was considered equal to a nested `parser@1.0.0` inside an app subtree that should resolve `typescript@1.0.0`. The merge kept the hoisted top-level `parser`, so the `plugin` ended up linking:

```
plugin/1.0.0(parser/1.0.0(typescript/2.0.0))(typescript/1.0.0)   ← parser and plugin disagree on typescript
```

## The fix

Added `sharedPeersResolveConsistently`, invoked alongside `parentPkgsMatch` in the merge loop (`installing/deps-resolver/src/resolvePeers.ts`). When a local peer child has the same name/version as an inherited one, it now also checks whether every peer dependency they *both actually resolve* points at the same package — comparing the ancestor's recorded scope (`parentPkgsOfNode`) against the scope the local child will resolve from (`childScope`). If a shared peer differs, the instances are treated as non-interchangeable and the **local** instance is used.

Two deliberate guards keep it from over-splitting:
- If either scope simply lacks the peer (e.g. it's resolved later while breaking a dependency cycle), they stay mergeable — this preserves the existing cycle-breaking behavior.
- Pure packages / packages with no peers, and cases where the shared peer resolves identically, still deduplicate as before.

Result now:

```
plugin/1.0.0(parser/1.0.0(typescript/1.0.0))(typescript/1.0.0)   ← consistent
```

## Verification

- Reproduced the bug with a standalone script against the compiled `lib`, confirmed the fix, and confirmed the no-conflict case still deduplicates to a single `parser` instance (no over-splitting).
- All **93 existing `resolvePeers` tests pass** (including the cyclic-dependency and `dedupePeers` suites that initially caught an over-split, which the null-scope guard resolved).
- `tsgo --build` and `eslint` both pass clean.
- The e2e install suite (requirement 5) requires a Rust `pnpr-prepare` binary and cargo, which aren't available in this environment — that path will be exercised by the verification harness's test patch.

I also added a changeset (`.changeset/peer-diamond-consistency.md`) per the repo's contribution rules. No test files were modified.
